title: Making a career
subtitle: apply, promote, resign, retire
summary: Tell the story of a working life - getting a job, promotion, resigning, unemployment, success and retirement.

lesson.heading: Getting a job
lesson.text: When you want a job you **apply for** it: you write a letter of **application** and send your **CV**, a document which describes your education and the jobs you have done. Then you have an **interview**, a meeting where someone asks you questions to see if you are suitable.

examples.text: When I left school, I **applied for** jobs in different companies.
I sent out lots of **CVs** and had some **interviews**.

examples.note: training = help and advice to learn how to do a job

lesson.note: You can also go on a training course or do a training course - a period of organised help and advice.

lesson.heading: Promotion
lesson.text: If you work hard, you may be **promoted**: given a better job with more responsibility. The noun is **promotion**. More money is a **pay rise**, and the knowledge you get from doing a job is **experience**.

examples.text: I worked hard and soon I **was promoted**.
They also gave me a good **pay rise**.
When my boss left, they gave me an important **promotion**.

lesson.heading: Resignation
lesson.text: **Resignation** is when you say officially that you are leaving a job. The verb is **resign**, and in everyday English we often say **quit**. If you work in another country, you **work abroad**.

examples.text: I **quit my job** and started looking for work in the UK.
examples.note: quit = resign, tell the company you are leaving

examples.text: She **resigned** when her boss refused to give her a pay rise.
I decided I wanted to **work abroad**.

lesson.heading: Unemployment
lesson.text: If a company tells you to leave, they **sack** you, or they **give you the sack**. Then you are **unemployed** - **out of work**. A **part-time job** is only part of the day or week; the opposite is a **full-time job**.

examples.text: After that I was **unemployed** for two months.
I got a **part-time job** in the kitchen of a restaurant.

lesson.heading: Success and retirement
lesson.text: If a business does well and makes money, it is **successful** - it is a **success**. The verb is **succeed**. If a restaurant belongs to you, it is your **own** restaurant and you are the **owner**. **Retirement** is the time when people stop work, often at 60 or 65.

examples.text: Three years later I opened my **own** restaurant.

examples.note: = it did well and made money

examples.text: Twenty years later I **owned** five restaurants and I was the **owner** of two hotels.
Last year, aged sixty, I **retired** and went back to Italy.

lesson.text: Training is uncountable: say *I had some training*, not ~~a training~~. But you can go on *a training course*.

exercises.prompt: Match each question with the best answer.

pairs.right: Because he was late for work every day.
Because he was the best person in the department.

pairs.left: Why did he apply for the job?
pairs.right: Because he was out of work.

pairs.left: Why did he quit his job?
pairs.right: Because he didn't like his boss.

pairs.left: Why did he go on the course?

exercises.prompt: I decided to work ___ to see what life was like in another country.
After they sacked me, I was out of ___ for six months.
exercises.explanation: To be out of work means to be unemployed.

exercises.prompt: I don't want a full-time job. I'd prefer to work ___.
exercises.explanation: A part-time job is only part of the day or week; the opposite is full time.

exercises.prompt: She ___ her job when her boss refused to give her a pay rise.
exercises.explanation: To quit a job means to resign - to tell the company you are leaving.

exercises.prompt: I didn't earn much money in the job, but it was still good ___ because I learned a lot.
exercises.explanation: Experience is the knowledge you get from doing something such as a job.

exercises.prompt: The company sent me on several training ___.
exercises.explanation: You go on or do a training course - a period of organised help and advice.

exercises.prompt: It's not easy to ___ in business; you need ability and luck.
exercises.explanation: The verb is succeed; the noun is success and the adjective is successful.

exercises.prompt: If you are interested in that job, you should definitely ___ for it.
exercises.explanation: You apply for a job by writing a letter of application.

exercises.prompt: Ivan was terrible as a tour guide; that's why they gave him the ___.
exercises.explanation: To give someone the sack means to tell them to leave the company.

exercises.prompt: I've worked for other people most of my life, but I'd really like to run my ___ company.
exercises.explanation: Your own company is a company that belongs to you.

exercises.prompt: If she's interested in that job, she'll have to write a letter of ___.
exercises.explanation: You apply for a job by sending a letter of application and your CV.

exercises.prompt: Put each word in the right column of its word family.

exercises.statement: I had a training when I joined the company.
exercises.explanation: Training is uncountable: I had some training when I joined the company.
